blocks.text:
(PN) quad-core quad-mode voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO)
which features magnetically reconﬁgurable (MR) technique and
fully symmetrical architecture. The MR technique, realized
through a transformer-based tank integrating an embedded
switched inductor, leverages varying core excitation currents to
achieve four distinct equivalent inductances, thereby enabling
quad-mode operation. This approach avoids the frequency tuning
range (FTR) compromise encountered when using capacitive
tuning elements in multi-mode tanks. Furthermore, the fully sym-
metrical characteristics of the inductive, capacitive, and active
elements, along with the routing layout, minimize mismatches
among the VCO cores, ensuring effective synchronization of
the four single-core VCOs and optimizing the PN in quad-core
operation. The proposed quad-core quad-mode VCO achieves an
FTR of 113.2% (4.21 to 15.18 GHz), a PN of −141.4 dBc/Hz at
a 10 MHz offset from 4.28 GHz, a peak ﬁgure-of-merit (FoM) of
190.5 dBc/Hz, a peak FoMT of 211.6 dBc/Hz and a peak FoMTA
of 220.5 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset.

area efﬁciency. However, as the number of operation modes
increases, transformer design becomes challenging and the
coupling network becomes complex, both of which tend to
introduce asymmetries across VCO cores. As a result, the
asymmetry induced by transformers or even other components
inevitably introduces frequency mismatches in multi-core
operation, which theoretically degrade the PN performance.
Therefore, a fully symmetrical architecture in multi-core multi-
mode VCOs are preferred to eliminate the negative impact on
the PN performance.

blocks.text:
quad-mode VCOs have been proposed in recent years. A dual-
core triple-mode VCO with a wide FTR of 80.6% and a PN of
−137.9 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset from 7.15 GHz is proposed
by using Electrical-Magnetic (E-M) mixed coupling in [15].
However, the asymmetrical inductance seen from each core
causes inter-core mismatches that degrades the PN. Moreover,
the inclusion of additional mode switches and switched capac-
itor arrays (SCAs) impose extra parasitics, thus reducing the
FTR. A quad-core quad-mode VCO in [22] achieves an FTR
of 101% and a PN of −133.2 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset
from 13.7 GHz by using E-M mixed coupling, whereas the
issue of asymmetrical inductance persists, and the parasitics
from electric coupling capacitors negatively impact the FTR.

is also undesirable. With the same total FTR, a uniform FTR

and 15. The adjacent and opposite coupling coefﬁcients, kadj
and kopp, are found to be 0.44 and 0.3 at 10 GHz, respectively.

inductor and the tank inductors is 0.49 at 10 GHz.

proposed design, a programmable tail resistor array is used
to adjust the current. In mode-1, a larger tail resistor is
used to moderate gm, while smaller resistors are employed
in modes-2 and -4 to allow higher gm. The VCO consumes
1.44 to 14.12 mW power under a VDD of 0.4 V, with
mode-1: 1.44–3.27 mW; mode-2: 9.51–13.46 mW; mode-3:
11.14–14.10 mW; and mode-4: 12.63–14.12 mW. Although
the 0.4 V low supply voltage helps reduce intrinsic power
consumption of the VCO, an on-chip regulator is typically
required to suppress noise and improve the power supply
rejection ratio (PSRR), which results in additional power
overhead. Across different modes, the Kpush of the proposed
VCO is measured to range from 126 to 297 MHz/V. Since
spur level depends on the PSRR, an on-chip regulator with
high PSRR is required to keep spurs low. Although magnetic
coupling brings Q variations, the tail resistor array ensures the
robust start-up and also suppresses ﬂicker noise up-conversion
across a wide FTR. This effect is reﬂected in the 1/f3 PN
corners in each mode, which span 35–220 kHz (mode-1), 130–
210 kHz (mode-2), 180–600 kHz (mode-3), and 90–750 kHz
(mode-4). A lower corner frequency indicates more effective
suppression of ﬂicker noise up-conversion. Thanks to the tail
resistor, the normalized PN (to 1 GHz) shows good ﬂatness
with minimal variations across the whole FTR, as shown in
Fig. 24(a). Moreover, Fig. 25 shows that the proposed VCO
exhibits the best overall performance in view of FoM and
FTR, and the best FoMTA in similar operating frequencies. The
results are compared with state-of-the-art wideband VCOs in
Table I, where the proposed VCO exhibits the largest FTR and
the largest FTR overlap facilitated by MR technique, validating
the robustness of the ultra-wide bandwidth.

blocks.text: V. CONCLUSION

lines.text: V. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: In this article, we present a quad-core quad-mode VCO

lines.text: In this article, we present a quad-core quad-mode VCO

spans.text: In this article, we present a quad-core quad-mode VCO

blocks.text:
featuring MR technique and fully symmetrical topology.
By changing the current directions of the tank inductors
via the mode-switching array and incorporating the switched
inductor, four distinct inductance values are realized, enabling
quad-mode operation without electrical coupling. Besides,
with careful consideration of the symmetry in the inductive,
capacitive, and active elements, as well as the routing layout,
mismatches among the VCO cores are signiﬁcantly minimized,
resulting in optimized PN performance. The VCO achieves
an FTR of 113.2% (4.21-to-15.18 GHz), a peak FoMT of
211.6 dBc/Hz and a peak FoMTA of 220.5 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz
offset.

1
A 4.21-to-15.18 GHz Magnetically Reconﬁgurable
and Fully Symmetrical Quad-Core Quad-Mode
VCO
Shijin Huang , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Pei Qin , Member, IEEE, Xiang Yi , Senior Member, IEEE,
Haoshen Zhu , Member, IEEE, Liang Wu , Member, IEEE, and Quan Xue , Fellow, IEEE

quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), voltage-controlled
oscillators (VCOs) are required to maintain low phase noise
(PN). However, achieving wide bandwidth and low PN simul-
taneously remains a signiﬁcant challenge for VCO designs.
Abstract— This work proposes a wideband low phase noise

(PN) quad-core quad-mode voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO)
which features magnetically reconﬁgurable (MR) technique and
fully symmetrical architecture. The MR technique, realized
through a transformer-based tank integrating an embedded
switched inductor, leverages varying core excitation currents to
achieve four distinct equivalent inductances, thereby enabling
quad-mode operation. This approach avoids the frequency tuning
range (FTR) compromise encountered when using capacitive
tuning elements in multi-mode tanks. Furthermore, the fully sym-
metrical characteristics of the inductive, capacitive, and active
elements, along with the routing layout, minimize mismatches
among the VCO cores, ensuring effective synchronization of
the four single-core VCOs and optimizing the PN in quad-core
operation. The proposed quad-core quad-mode VCO achieves an
FTR of 113.2% (4.21 to 15.18 GHz), a PN of −141.4 dBc/Hz at
a 10 MHz offset from 4.28 GHz, a peak ﬁgure-of-merit (FoM) of
190.5 dBc/Hz, a peak FoMT of 211.6 dBc/Hz and a peak FoMTA
of 220.5 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset.
Compared to the scheme that uses multiple individual

VCOs for multi-band operation, mode-switching technique
summarized in [1] provides a more efﬁcient solution, enabling
multi-band coverage with reduced area and lower power con-
sumption. The switched-inductors or switched-transformers
techniques are favorable to achieve wide bandwidth by utiliz-
ing multiple effective inductance values [2], [3], [4]. Although
these techniques can broaden the bandwidth effectively in a
simple manner, the ON-resistance of the switches degrades the
Q factor of the tank, thus signiﬁcantly deteriorating the PN.

Recently, coupling multiple VCO cores operating at different
modes via mode switches has been demonstrated to be a
promising method to simultaneously achieve low PN and wide
FTR.

In multi-core multi-mode VCOs, transformer-based res-

onant tanks are preferred for their design ﬂexibility and
area efﬁciency. However, as the number of operation modes
increases, transformer design becomes challenging and the
coupling network becomes complex, both of which tend to
introduce asymmetries across VCO cores. As a result, the
asymmetry induced by transformers or even other components
inevitably introduces frequency mismatches in multi-core
operation, which theoretically degrade the PN performance.
Therefore, a fully symmetrical architecture in multi-core multi-
mode VCOs are preferred to eliminate the negative impact on
the PN performance.
A substantial number of state-of-the-art triple-mode or

quad-mode VCOs have been proposed in recent years. A dual-
core triple-mode VCO with a wide FTR of 80.6% and a PN of
−137.9 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset from 7.15 GHz is proposed
by using Electrical-Magnetic (E-M) mixed coupling in [15].
However, the asymmetrical inductance seen from each core
causes inter-core mismatches that degrades the PN. Moreover,
the inclusion of additional mode switches and switched capac-
itor arrays (SCAs) impose extra parasitics, thus reducing the
FTR. A quad-core quad-mode VCO in [22] achieves an FTR
of 101% and a PN of −133.2 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset
from 13.7 GHz by using E-M mixed coupling, whereas the
issue of asymmetrical inductance persists, and the parasitics
from electric coupling capacitors negatively impact the FTR.
Additionally, the non-uniformity of the FTR across each mode
is also undesirable. With the same total FTR, a uniform FTR

This gives rise to two concerns. First, large differences in

parasitic-induced FTR reduction, and nonuniform FTR still
persist, ultimately degrading the overall performance of the

To surmount these issues, this work proposes a quad-

core quad-mode VCO that achieves ultra-wide bandwidth and
low PN by employing MR technique and fully symmetric
architecture, which effectively eliminates the asymmetry and
extra parasitics, and ensures a uniform FTR across all modes.
This article is organized as follows. Section II presents the
structure of the proposed VCO and the operating principles
of the four modes. Section III discusses the symmetry of
the design and its optimization of performance. Section IV
presents the measurement results and Section V draws the

the same frequency. This process, however, degrades the
tank Q and renders the theoretical 6 dB PN optimization
from the quad-core operation unachievable. Therefore,
this mode is abandoned.

are controlled by 5-bit control bits, respectively. In mode-1,
Groups-1 and -2 are activated; in mode-2, Groups-1, -2, and -5
are active. Mode-3 enables Group-1 and -3, whereas mode-4

enables Group-3 and -4. Unless otherwise speciﬁed, all other
switch groups remain disabled.
Given the careful consideration of the symmetry of the

inductive, capacitive, active, and other elements in the quad-
core quad-mode VCO, the mismatches among VCO cores are
signiﬁcantly minimized, allowing the four single-core VCOs to
be well synchronized and achieve optimized PN in all modes.
B. Avoiding Mode Ambiguity
It is known that when the transconductance pairs are sufﬁ-

ciently large, the oscillator operates at the frequency where the
tank impedance provides sufﬁciently high amplitude with zero
phase. When no mode switches are added or the switch size is
too small [i.e., large ON-resistance (RON)], multiple frequency
points with high impedance amplitude and zero phase may
exist. As a result, the operating frequency of the oscillator is
not uniquely deﬁned, resulting in mode ambiguity.
Due to the symmetrical property of the proposed trans-
former, the tank impedance seen from node pairs P1 and
P2, P3 and P4, P5 and P6, P7 and P8 is identical. Fig. 14

shows the simulated magnitude and phase responses of the
tank impedance seen from the node pair P1 and P2 in the four
operation modes, as RON is reduced from 425 to 25 . When
RON is 225/425 , as shown by the blue/green dotted curve

in Fig. 14, each mode exhibits at least two frequency points
where the tank impedance has a sufﬁciently high peak and a
zero phase. This implies that the oscillator has the potential to
oscillate either at the frequency with the expected maximum
Q value or concurrently at multiple resonance frequencies,
which are highly undesirable.
To avoid the issues associated with ambiguous modes, it is

necessary to reduce RON by increasing the size of the mode
switches. As shown by the solid red curves in Fig. 14, when
RON is reduced to 25 , each mode exhibits a uniquely deﬁned
resonant frequency.

C. Effect of Mismatches Among Cores
While ideal synchronization assumes identical oscillation

frequencies among the cores, practical implementations often
suffer from frequency mismatches caused by device variations
and layout asymmetries. These mismatches introduce phase
errors and amplitude reduction, ultimately degrading the PN
performance [21], [27]. Therefore, accurately characterizing
and mitigating inter-core mismatches are essential to fully
unlock the potential of multi-core VCO designs.
The proposed design makes every effort to ensure symmetry

among the four VCO cores, including the transformer tank,
SW
array, VCO cores and layout routings. As presented in

Fig. 9(a), each single tank inductor is identical and arranged
in a centrally symmetric layout. Additionally, the SW array,
consisting of sixteen switches, is also arranged in a center-
symmetric conﬁguration, as illustrated in Fig. 15. That is to
say, each port (P1−8) is identically connected to four switches
to ensure that the parasitics induced by the switches is the
same across all ports. Moreover, each VCO core is connected
to the SW array by identical routings, and synchronized with
other three cores directly through the SW array, thus further
reducing frequency mismatches and mitigating its impact on
the VCO performance.
However, due to the presence of the switched inductor,

as shown in Fig. 9(a), the effective inductances seen by core-

IV. MEASUREMENT RESULTS
The proposed quad-core quad-mode VCO is implemented

in 65 nm bulk CMOS with a core chip area of 0.152 mm2,
as shown in Fig. 21. Fig. 22 shows the measured PN at 4.28,
8.66, 11.57, and 15.07 GHz, respectively, from four distinct
modes. The measured FTR is 113.2% (4.21–15.18 GHz), with
the frequency in each mode ranging from 4.21 to 6.24 GHz,
5.62 to 8.66 GHz, 7.52 to 11.6 GHz, and 10.01 to 15.18 GHz,
respectively, as shown in Fig. 23. In each mode, the tuning
voltage ranges from 0 to 2.5 V. It’s worth noting that the
minimum frequency overlap between two adjacent modes is
10.5%, which further validates the robustness of the wide
bandwidth. We further report the VCO gain KVCO on this
plot at Vtune = 1.2 V . Fig. 24(a) and (b) show the measured
PN, FoM and FoMT over the whole FTR, respectively, where
the PN is from −108.8 to −120.3 dBc/Hz and −130.7 to
−141.4 dBc/Hz at 1 and 10 MHz offsets while the FoM

and FoMT vary from 180.0 to 190.5 dBc/Hz and 201.1 to
211.6 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset.
The tank’s effective parallel resistance RT varies by mode,

owing to variations in Q across modes. Since mode-1 exhibits
the largest Q and thus the largest RT , it requires the smallest
gm and hence the lowest current consumption, while the
higher frequency and lower Q modes require more. In the
proposed design, a programmable tail resistor array is used
to adjust the current. In mode-1, a larger tail resistor is
used to moderate gm, while smaller resistors are employed
in modes-2 and -4 to allow higher gm. The VCO consumes
1.44 to 14.12 mW power under a VDD of 0.4 V, with
mode-1: 1.44–3.27 mW; mode-2: 9.51–13.46 mW; mode-3:
11.14–14.10 mW; and mode-4: 12.63–14.12 mW. Although
the 0.4 V low supply voltage helps reduce intrinsic power
consumption of the VCO, an on-chip regulator is typically
required to suppress noise and improve the power supply
rejection ratio (PSRR), which results in additional power
overhead. Across different modes, the Kpush of the proposed
VCO is measured to range from 126 to 297 MHz/V. Since
spur level depends on the PSRR, an on-chip regulator with
high PSRR is required to keep spurs low. Although magnetic
coupling brings Q variations, the tail resistor array ensures the
robust start-up and also suppresses ﬂicker noise up-conversion
across a wide FTR. This effect is reﬂected in the 1/f3 PN
corners in each mode, which span 35–220 kHz (mode-1), 130–
210 kHz (mode-2), 180–600 kHz (mode-3), and 90–750 kHz
(mode-4). A lower corner frequency indicates more effective
suppression of ﬂicker noise up-conversion. Thanks to the tail
resistor, the normalized PN (to 1 GHz) shows good ﬂatness
with minimal variations across the whole FTR, as shown in
Fig. 24(a). Moreover, Fig. 25 shows that the proposed VCO
exhibits the best overall performance in view of FoM and
FTR, and the best FoMTA in similar operating frequencies. The
results are compared with state-of-the-art wideband VCOs in
Table I, where the proposed VCO exhibits the largest FTR and
the largest FTR overlap facilitated by MR technique, validating
the robustness of the ultra-wide bandwidth.
V. CONCLUSION
In this article, we present a quad-core quad-mode VCO

featuring MR technique and fully symmetrical topology.
By changing the current directions of the tank inductors
via the mode-switching array and incorporating the switched
inductor, four distinct inductance values are realized, enabling
quad-mode operation without electrical coupling. Besides,
with careful consideration of the symmetry in the inductive,
capacitive, and active elements, as well as the routing layout,
mismatches among the VCO cores are signiﬁcantly minimized,
resulting in optimized PN performance. The VCO achieves
an FTR of 113.2% (4.21-to-15.18 GHz), a peak FoMT of
211.6 dBc/Hz and a peak FoMTA of 220.5 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz
offset.

quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), voltage-controlled
oscillators (VCOs) are required to maintain low phase noise
(PN). However, achieving wide bandwidth and low PN simul-
taneously remains a signiﬁcant challenge for VCO designs.
Compared to the scheme that uses multiple individual

VCOs for multi-band operation, mode-switching technique
summarized in [1] provides a more efﬁcient solution, enabling
multi-band coverage with reduced area and lower power con-
sumption. The switched-inductors or switched-transformers
techniques are favorable to achieve wide bandwidth by utiliz-
ing multiple effective inductance values [2], [3], [4]. Although
these techniques can broaden the bandwidth effectively in a
simple manner, the ON-resistance of the switches degrades the
Q factor of the tank, thus signiﬁcantly deteriorating the PN.

Recently, coupling multiple VCO cores operating at different
modes via mode switches has been demonstrated to be a
promising method to simultaneously achieve low PN and wide
FTR.
Based on Leeson’s PN model [5], the PN can be expressed

where k is Boltzmann’s constant, T is the absolute tempera-
ture, F is the device excess noise factor, V0 is the oscillation
amplitude, RT is the tank resistance, and Q is the tank
quality factor. Coupling N VCO cores results in a 10logN
dB PN reduction, as RT in (1) is reduced by a factor of
N while other parameters remain ﬁxed. However, this PN

performance improvement comes at the cost of an N-fold
increase in power consumption. By utilizing mode switches
among the multiple VCO cores, multiple operation modes
can be generated, extending the FTR without incurring switch
losses.
Dual-mode VCOs have been widely reported [6], [7], [8],

[9], [10], [11], [12], [13], which employ either magnetically
reconﬁgurable (MR) inductance (denoted “M”) or electric cou-
pling via added capacitors to change the effective capacitance
(denoted “E”) to realize dual-mode operation. While an octave
tuning range can theoretically be divided or multiplied to
target any frequency band, dual-mode VCOs typically struggle
to achieve full octave coverage due to practical limitations.
As a result, triple-mode [14], [15], [16], [17] or even quad-
mode VCOs [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24] have

gained popularity. In order to expand the number of operation
modes, MR technique is typically combined with electric
coupling. However, the latter introduces substantial parasitic
capacitance, which increases Cmin and consequently reduces
the FTR, expressed as follows:

where Cmin and Cmax denote the minimum and maximum val-
ues of the tank capacitance, respectively. Thus, MR technique
is favored in those multi-core multi-mode VCO designs.
In multi-core multi-mode VCOs, transformer-based res-

onant tanks are preferred for their design ﬂexibility and
area efﬁciency. However, as the number of operation modes
increases, transformer design becomes challenging and the
coupling network becomes complex, both of which tend to
introduce asymmetries across VCO cores. As a result, the
asymmetry induced by transformers or even other components
inevitably introduces frequency mismatches in multi-core
operation, which theoretically degrade the PN performance.
Therefore, a fully symmetrical architecture in multi-core multi-
mode VCOs are preferred to eliminate the negative impact on
the PN performance.
A substantial number of state-of-the-art triple-mode or

quad-mode VCOs have been proposed in recent years. A dual-
core triple-mode VCO with a wide FTR of 80.6% and a PN of
−137.9 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset from 7.15 GHz is proposed
by using Electrical-Magnetic (E-M) mixed coupling in [15].
However, the asymmetrical inductance seen from each core
causes inter-core mismatches that degrades the PN. Moreover,
the inclusion of additional mode switches and switched capac-
itor arrays (SCAs) impose extra parasitics, thus reducing the
FTR. A quad-core quad-mode VCO in [22] achieves an FTR
of 101% and a PN of −133.2 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset
from 13.7 GHz by using E-M mixed coupling, whereas the
issue of asymmetrical inductance persists, and the parasitics
from electric coupling capacitors negatively impact the FTR.
Additionally, the non-uniformity of the FTR across each mode
is also undesirable. With the same total FTR, a uniform FTR

in each mode yields roughly equal overlaps between adjacent
modes, as shown in Fig. 1(a). In contrast, a nonuniform FTR
makes the overlaps highly uneven, as shown in Fig. 1(b).
This gives rise to two concerns. First, large differences in
overlap make the band-decision thresholds difﬁcult to unify
and require additional algorithm adaptation, which increases
system complexity. Second, under PVT variations, the smaller
overlap is more likely to shrink and create a frequency gap
between adjacent modes. Other works still suffer from these
issues [18], [21]. In summary, although multi-core multi-
mode VCOs have demonstrated superior performance in terms
of FTR and PN, issues such as asymmetrical inductance,
parasitic-induced FTR reduction, and nonuniform FTR still
persist, ultimately degrading the overall performance of the
VCOs.
To surmount these issues, this work proposes a quad-

core quad-mode VCO that achieves ultra-wide bandwidth and
low PN by employing MR technique and fully symmetric
architecture, which effectively eliminates the asymmetry and
extra parasitics, and ensures a uniform FTR across all modes.
This article is organized as follows. Section II presents the
structure of the proposed VCO and the operating principles
of the four modes. Section III discusses the symmetry of
the design and its optimization of performance. Section IV
presents the measurement results and Section V draws the
conclusion.

items.text: quad-mode VCO, which consists of four identical single-core

VCOs, an embedded switched inductor (Lsw) and a mode-
switching (SW) array. The active cores (Core-1, -2, -3, and
-4), each composed of cross-coupled transistors, a tail resistor
array, a pair of varactors and 6-bit SCA, are identical. The
tail resistor array, shown in the bottom-left of Fig. 13(a),
consists of a bypass path and a 13-bit programmable resistor
bank. It is added to tune the core transconductance Gm versus
frequency so that the excess loop gain G X = Gm RT (with
RT the tank’s equivalent parallel resistance) remains moderate,

which in turn limits ﬂicker noise up-conversion [26]. The 6-
bit SCA, shown in the top-left of Fig. 13(a), and the MOS
varactors provide coarse tuning and continuous ﬁne tuning,
respectively. The varactor is implemented using a thick-oxide
device, with dimensions of W/L = 32/0.4 μm. As the bias
increases from 0 to 2.5 V, the varactor capacitance decreases
from 35.7 to 15.2 fF (C = 20.5 fF) with Q larger than
29. The SCA exhibits an LSB of 7.7 fF, thereby enabling
ﬁne and continuous frequency tuning. With a high Cmax/Cmin
ratio preserved and Q kept moderate, the total capacitance
ranges from 191.9 to 732.1 fF, and Q remains above 24 at
10 GHz. Each core is connected to its respective inductor ports
in a center-symmetric manner, ensuring uniform coupling and
balanced performance across all modes.
Furthermore, to maintain uniform capacitive loading at each

port, the SW array is designed with four identical sub-arrays,
all positioned at the center of the transformer symmetrically.
Each sub-array contains four switches and there are a total
of sixteen switches in all. An additional switch is positioned
along the routing of the switched inductor to control its on/off
state. As discussed above, eight switches need to be turned on
and another eight switches need to be turned off in each mode.
The switch on-off states in each mode are shown in Fig. 13(b).
As observed, these switches are divided into ﬁve groups and
are controlled by 5-bit control bits, respectively. In mode-1,
Groups-1 and -2 are activated; in mode-2, Groups-1, -2, and -5
are active. Mode-3 enables Group-1 and -3, whereas mode-4

enables Group-3 and -4. Unless otherwise speciﬁed, all other
switch groups remain disabled.
Given the careful consideration of the symmetry of the

inductive, capacitive, active, and other elements in the quad-
core quad-mode VCO, the mismatches among VCO cores are
signiﬁcantly minimized, allowing the four single-core VCOs to
be well synchronized and achieve optimized PN in all modes.

items.text: It is known that when the transconductance pairs are sufﬁ-

ciently large, the oscillator operates at the frequency where the
tank impedance provides sufﬁciently high amplitude with zero

frequencies among the cores, practical implementations often
suffer from frequency mismatches caused by device variations
and layout asymmetries. These mismatches introduce phase
errors and amplitude reduction, ultimately degrading the PN
performance [21], [27]. Therefore, accurately characterizing
and mitigating inter-core mismatches are essential to fully
unlock the potential of multi-core VCO designs.

In the proposed design, the asymmetry caused by the

we now examine the inﬂuence of RON on PN in the absence
of frequency mismatch. Following the derivation in [29], the
PN expression for a symmetrical quad-core VCO is given by

Comparing (31) with (1), it is evident that (31) contains an
additional factor m, expressed as follows:
It can be observed that both RON and ω have an impact
on the PN improvement. When RON is much smaller than
ZT (ω), the value of m is approximately 1/4 and the PN

is improved by approximately 6 dB compared to a single-
core VCO. On the other hand, in the case when RON is much
larger than ZT (ω) (i.e., m ≈1), the PN approaches that of
a single-core VCO, indicating that the four oscillator cores are
no longer frequency-locked and instead operate as independent
PERFORMANCE SUMMARY AND COMPARISON WITH STATE-OF-THE-ART OSCILLATORS

free-running oscillators. Fig. 20 illustrates the calculated PN
degradation of the proposed VCO with RON = 25  across
all four modes as a function of frequency offsets, based
on (28). The PN degradation is nearly zero, thus a near-
6 dB PN reduction is still achieved. Relatively speaking,
mode-1 exhibits the most severe degradation, but even at
a 100 MHz offset, the degradation is less than 0.035 dB,
which demonstrates excellent synchronization performance of
the proposed quad-core VCO.
The proposed quad-core quad-mode VCO is implemented

in 65 nm bulk CMOS with a core chip area of 0.152 mm2,
as shown in Fig. 21. Fig. 22 shows the measured PN at 4.28,
8.66, 11.57, and 15.07 GHz, respectively, from four distinct
modes. The measured FTR is 113.2% (4.21–15.18 GHz), with
the frequency in each mode ranging from 4.21 to 6.24 GHz,
5.62 to 8.66 GHz, 7.52 to 11.6 GHz, and 10.01 to 15.18 GHz,
respectively, as shown in Fig. 23. In each mode, the tuning
voltage ranges from 0 to 2.5 V. It’s worth noting that the
minimum frequency overlap between two adjacent modes is
10.5%, which further validates the robustness of the wide
bandwidth. We further report the VCO gain KVCO on this
plot at Vtune = 1.2 V . Fig. 24(a) and (b) show the measured
PN, FoM and FoMT over the whole FTR, respectively, where
the PN is from −108.8 to −120.3 dBc/Hz and −130.7 to
−141.4 dBc/Hz at 1 and 10 MHz offsets while the FoM

and FoMT vary from 180.0 to 190.5 dBc/Hz and 201.1 to
211.6 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset.
The tank’s effective parallel resistance RT varies by mode,

owing to variations in Q across modes. Since mode-1 exhibits
the largest Q and thus the largest RT , it requires the smallest
gm and hence the lowest current consumption, while the
higher frequency and lower Q modes require more. In the
proposed design, a programmable tail resistor array is used
to adjust the current. In mode-1, a larger tail resistor is
used to moderate gm, while smaller resistors are employed
in modes-2 and -4 to allow higher gm. The VCO consumes
1.44 to 14.12 mW power under a VDD of 0.4 V, with
mode-1: 1.44–3.27 mW; mode-2: 9.51–13.46 mW; mode-3:
11.14–14.10 mW; and mode-4: 12.63–14.12 mW. Although
the 0.4 V low supply voltage helps reduce intrinsic power
consumption of the VCO, an on-chip regulator is typically
required to suppress noise and improve the power supply
rejection ratio (PSRR), which results in additional power
overhead. Across different modes, the Kpush of the proposed
VCO is measured to range from 126 to 297 MHz/V. Since
spur level depends on the PSRR, an on-chip regulator with
high PSRR is required to keep spurs low. Although magnetic
coupling brings Q variations, the tail resistor array ensures the
robust start-up and also suppresses ﬂicker noise up-conversion
across a wide FTR. This effect is reﬂected in the 1/f3 PN
corners in each mode, which span 35–220 kHz (mode-1), 130–
210 kHz (mode-2), 180–600 kHz (mode-3), and 90–750 kHz
(mode-4). A lower corner frequency indicates more effective
suppression of ﬂicker noise up-conversion. Thanks to the tail
resistor, the normalized PN (to 1 GHz) shows good ﬂatness
with minimal variations across the whole FTR, as shown in
Fig. 24(a). Moreover, Fig. 25 shows that the proposed VCO
exhibits the best overall performance in view of FoM and
FTR, and the best FoMTA in similar operating frequencies. The
results are compared with state-of-the-art wideband VCOs in
Table I, where the proposed VCO exhibits the largest FTR and
the largest FTR overlap facilitated by MR technique, validating
the robustness of the ultra-wide bandwidth.
In this article, we present a quad-core quad-mode VCO

featuring MR technique and fully symmetrical topology.
By changing the current directions of the tank inductors
via the mode-switching array and incorporating the switched
inductor, four distinct inductance values are realized, enabling
quad-mode operation without electrical coupling. Besides,
with careful consideration of the symmetry in the inductive,
capacitive, and active elements, as well as the routing layout,
mismatches among the VCO cores are signiﬁcantly minimized,
resulting in optimized PN performance. The VCO achieves
an FTR of 113.2% (4.21-to-15.18 GHz), a peak FoMT of
211.6 dBc/Hz and a peak FoMTA of 220.5 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz
offset.

Abstract— This work proposes a wideband low phase noise

(PN) quad-core quad-mode voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO)
which features magnetically reconﬁgurable (MR) technique and
fully symmetrical architecture. The MR technique, realized
through a transformer-based tank integrating an embedded
switched inductor, leverages varying core excitation currents to
achieve four distinct equivalent inductances, thereby enabling
quad-mode operation. This approach avoids the frequency tuning
range (FTR) compromise encountered when using capacitive
tuning elements in multi-mode tanks. Furthermore, the fully sym-
metrical characteristics of the inductive, capacitive, and active
elements, along with the routing layout, minimize mismatches
among the VCO cores, ensuring effective synchronization of
the four single-core VCOs and optimizing the PN in quad-core
operation. The proposed quad-core quad-mode VCO achieves an
FTR of 113.2% (4.21 to 15.18 GHz), a PN of −141.4 dBc/Hz at
a 10 MHz offset from 4.28 GHz, a peak ﬁgure-of-merit (FoM) of
190.5 dBc/Hz, a peak FoMT of 211.6 dBc/Hz and a peak FoMTA
of 220.5 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset.
Index Terms— Magnetically reconﬁgurable (MR), phase noise

(PN), quad-core, quad-mode, voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO),
wide frequency tuning range (FTR).

application scenarios in 5G communications, a local

oscillator (LO) with wide frequency tuning range (FTR)
is urgently desired. Besides, with the increasing demand
for signal purity in high-order modulation schemes such as

quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), voltage-controlled
oscillators (VCOs) are required to maintain low phase noise
(PN). However, achieving wide bandwidth and low PN simul-
taneously remains a signiﬁcant challenge for VCO designs.
Compared to the scheme that uses multiple individual

VCOs for multi-band operation, mode-switching technique
summarized in [1] provides a more efﬁcient solution, enabling
multi-band coverage with reduced area and lower power con-
sumption. The switched-inductors or switched-transformers
techniques are favorable to achieve wide bandwidth by utiliz-
ing multiple effective inductance values [2], [3], [4]. Although
these techniques can broaden the bandwidth effectively in a
simple manner, the ON-resistance of the switches degrades the
Q factor of the tank, thus signiﬁcantly deteriorating the PN.

Recently, coupling multiple VCO cores operating at different
modes via mode switches has been demonstrated to be a
promising method to simultaneously achieve low PN and wide
FTR.
Based on Leeson’s PN model [5], the PN can be expressed

where k is Boltzmann’s constant, T is the absolute tempera-
ture, F is the device excess noise factor, V0 is the oscillation
amplitude, RT is the tank resistance, and Q is the tank
quality factor. Coupling N VCO cores results in a 10logN
dB PN reduction, as RT in (1) is reduced by a factor of
N while other parameters remain ﬁxed. However, this PN

performance improvement comes at the cost of an N-fold
increase in power consumption. By utilizing mode switches
among the multiple VCO cores, multiple operation modes
can be generated, extending the FTR without incurring switch
losses.
Dual-mode VCOs have been widely reported [6], [7], [8],

[9], [10], [11], [12], [13], which employ either magnetically
reconﬁgurable (MR) inductance (denoted “M”) or electric cou-
pling via added capacitors to change the effective capacitance
(denoted “E”) to realize dual-mode operation. While an octave
tuning range can theoretically be divided or multiplied to
target any frequency band, dual-mode VCOs typically struggle
to achieve full octave coverage due to practical limitations.
As a result, triple-mode [14], [15], [16], [17] or even quad-
mode VCOs [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24] have

gained popularity. In order to expand the number of operation
modes, MR technique is typically combined with electric
coupling. However, the latter introduces substantial parasitic
capacitance, which increases Cmin and consequently reduces
the FTR, expressed as follows:

where Cmin and Cmax denote the minimum and maximum val-
ues of the tank capacitance, respectively. Thus, MR technique
is favored in those multi-core multi-mode VCO designs.
In multi-core multi-mode VCOs, transformer-based res-

onant tanks are preferred for their design ﬂexibility and
area efﬁciency. However, as the number of operation modes
increases, transformer design becomes challenging and the
coupling network becomes complex, both of which tend to
introduce asymmetries across VCO cores. As a result, the
asymmetry induced by transformers or even other components
inevitably introduces frequency mismatches in multi-core
operation, which theoretically degrade the PN performance.
Therefore, a fully symmetrical architecture in multi-core multi-
mode VCOs are preferred to eliminate the negative impact on
the PN performance.
A substantial number of state-of-the-art triple-mode or

quad-mode VCOs have been proposed in recent years. A dual-
core triple-mode VCO with a wide FTR of 80.6% and a PN of
−137.9 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset from 7.15 GHz is proposed
by using Electrical-Magnetic (E-M) mixed coupling in [15].
However, the asymmetrical inductance seen from each core
causes inter-core mismatches that degrades the PN. Moreover,
the inclusion of additional mode switches and switched capac-
itor arrays (SCAs) impose extra parasitics, thus reducing the
FTR. A quad-core quad-mode VCO in [22] achieves an FTR
of 101% and a PN of −133.2 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset
from 13.7 GHz by using E-M mixed coupling, whereas the
issue of asymmetrical inductance persists, and the parasitics
from electric coupling capacitors negatively impact the FTR.
Additionally, the non-uniformity of the FTR across each mode
is also undesirable. With the same total FTR, a uniform FTR

in each mode yields roughly equal overlaps between adjacent
modes, as shown in Fig. 1(a). In contrast, a nonuniform FTR
makes the overlaps highly uneven, as shown in Fig. 1(b).
This gives rise to two concerns. First, large differences in
overlap make the band-decision thresholds difﬁcult to unify
and require additional algorithm adaptation, which increases
system complexity. Second, under PVT variations, the smaller
overlap is more likely to shrink and create a frequency gap
between adjacent modes. Other works still suffer from these
issues [18], [21]. In summary, although multi-core multi-
mode VCOs have demonstrated superior performance in terms
of FTR and PN, issues such as asymmetrical inductance,
parasitic-induced FTR reduction, and nonuniform FTR still
persist, ultimately degrading the overall performance of the
VCOs.
To surmount these issues, this work proposes a quad-

core quad-mode VCO that achieves ultra-wide bandwidth and
low PN by employing MR technique and fully symmetric
architecture, which effectively eliminates the asymmetry and
extra parasitics, and ensures a uniform FTR across all modes.
This article is organized as follows. Section II presents the
structure of the proposed VCO and the operating principles
of the four modes. Section III discusses the symmetry of
the design and its optimization of performance. Section IV
presents the measurement results and Section V draws the
conclusion.
Dual-core dual-mode VCO serves as the foundational archi-

tecture for multi-core multi-mode VCO designs, as shown
in Fig. 2. By controlling the phases of the two coupled
inductors through the mode switches SO and SE, two effective
inductances are achieved, thereby realizing two operation
modes, namely odd mode and even mode. Fig. 3 shows the
quad-core triple-mode conﬁguration derived from the dual-
core dual-mode structure. It simply connects four single VCO
cores through mode switches, with the key difference that

the inductors of the four cores are mutually coupled with
each other. Besides, to ensure symmetry among the cores,
the coupling coefﬁcients between adjacent inductors and those
between the opposite inductors are equal, resulting in the
relationship as follows:
The sixteen mode switches (Si, j) are employed to connect

the corresponding two ports (Pi, Pj). By changing the current
directions of the tank inductors in each core through the mode
switches, the proposed VCO can operate in three resonant
modes. The three operation modes are described as follows.
1) In mode-L, as shown in Fig. 4(a), the current directions
of four tank inductors are all in-phase, with the switches

Speciﬁcally, for core-1, the magnetic inﬂuence from

3) In mode-H, as shown in Fig. 4(c), the currents in

cores and Mopp from the opposite core, resulting in the

Since Lmode,M −Lmode,H is equal to 2(Madj −Mopp)
and Madj is set larger than Mopp in this design, mode-M
is thus operating at a lower frequency.
4) In mode-N, as shown in Fig. 4(d), the current in any

given core is anti-phase with other three cores, with the
switches S1,4, S1,6, S2,3, S2,5, S3,8, S4,7, S5,8, and S6,7
turned on. Based on the current direction in each core,
the effective inductance of each core can be derived as
L + Mopp for core-1 and -4, L + 2Madj −Mopp for

core-2, and L −2Madj −Mopp for core-3. Unlike the
other three modes, where the effective inductor for each
core is identical, the inductance seen from each core
in this mode is varied, leading to signiﬁcant frequency
mismatches among four cores. In a multi-core VCO,
all cores should be typically designed to be identical to
ensure balanced operation. This mismatch in inductance
will lead to unequal current distribution among the
cores, which in turn causes imbalances in the waveforms
among VCO cores. Then the current will ﬂowthrough
the lossy switches in order to equalize the energy of
the resonators, thereby forcing the VCO to oscillate at
the same frequency. This process, however, degrades the
tank Q and renders the theoretical 6 dB PN optimization
from the quad-core operation unachievable. Therefore,
this mode is abandoned.
In summary, three distinct equivalent inductance values
are realized through a fully symmetrical transformer
network composed of four mutually coupled inductors.
However, since the difference Lmode,L −Lmode,M exceeds

frequency tuning between mode-M and -H may result
in a frequency gap between mode-L and -M. Therefore,
an additional mode inserted between mode-L and -M is
required, which should minimally affect other modes.
Based on the triple-mode transformer in Fig. 3, a switched

inductor is embedded within the four tank inductors, as shown
in Fig. 5, thereby creating one additional mode. The switched
inductor operates in two different states, depending on its
connection state.
1) 1) When the switched inductor Lsw is turned off, three

increases from 0 to 2.5 V, the varactor capacitance decreases
from 35.7 to 15.2 fF (C = 20.5 fF) with Q larger than
29. The SCA exhibits an LSB of 7.7 fF, thereby enabling
ﬁne and continuous frequency tuning. With a high Cmax/Cmin
ratio preserved and Q kept moderate, the total capacitance
ranges from 191.9 to 732.1 fF, and Q remains above 24 at
10 GHz. Each core is connected to its respective inductor ports
in a center-symmetric manner, ensuring uniform coupling and
balanced performance across all modes.
Furthermore, to maintain uniform capacitive loading at each

port, the SW array is designed with four identical sub-arrays,
all positioned at the center of the transformer symmetrically.
Each sub-array contains four switches and there are a total
of sixteen switches in all. An additional switch is positioned
along the routing of the switched inductor to control its on/off
state. As discussed above, eight switches need to be turned on
and another eight switches need to be turned off in each mode.
The switch on-off states in each mode are shown in Fig. 13(b).
As observed, these switches are divided into ﬁve groups and
are controlled by 5-bit control bits, respectively. In mode-1,
Groups-1 and -2 are activated; in mode-2, Groups-1, -2, and -5
are active. Mode-3 enables Group-1 and -3, whereas mode-4

enables Group-3 and -4. Unless otherwise speciﬁed, all other
switch groups remain disabled.
Given the careful consideration of the symmetry of the

inductive, capacitive, active, and other elements in the quad-
core quad-mode VCO, the mismatches among VCO cores are
signiﬁcantly minimized, allowing the four single-core VCOs to
be well synchronized and achieve optimized PN in all modes.

exist. As a result, the operating frequency of the oscillator is
not uniquely deﬁned, resulting in mode ambiguity.

The tank’s effective parallel resistance RT varies by mode,

owing to variations in Q across modes. Since mode-1 exhibits
the largest Q and thus the largest RT , it requires the smallest
gm and hence the lowest current consumption, while the
higher frequency and lower Q modes require more. In the
proposed design, a programmable tail resistor array is used
to adjust the current. In mode-1, a larger tail resistor is
used to moderate gm, while smaller resistors are employed
in modes-2 and -4 to allow higher gm. The VCO consumes
1.44 to 14.12 mW power under a VDD of 0.4 V, with
mode-1: 1.44–3.27 mW; mode-2: 9.51–13.46 mW; mode-3:
11.14–14.10 mW; and mode-4: 12.63–14.12 mW. Although
the 0.4 V low supply voltage helps reduce intrinsic power
consumption of the VCO, an on-chip regulator is typically
required to suppress noise and improve the power supply
rejection ratio (PSRR), which results in additional power
overhead. Across different modes, the Kpush of the proposed
VCO is measured to range from 126 to 297 MHz/V. Since
spur level depends on the PSRR, an on-chip regulator with
high PSRR is required to keep spurs low. Although magnetic
coupling brings Q variations, the tail resistor array ensures the
robust start-up and also suppresses ﬂicker noise up-conversion
across a wide FTR. This effect is reﬂected in the 1/f3 PN
corners in each mode, which span 35–220 kHz (mode-1), 130–
210 kHz (mode-2), 180–600 kHz (mode-3), and 90–750 kHz
(mode-4). A lower corner frequency indicates more effective
suppression of ﬂicker noise up-conversion. Thanks to the tail
resistor, the normalized PN (to 1 GHz) shows good ﬂatness
with minimal variations across the whole FTR, as shown in
Fig. 24(a). Moreover, Fig. 25 shows that the proposed VCO
exhibits the best overall performance in view of FoM and
FTR, and the best FoMTA in similar operating frequencies. The
results are compared with state-of-the-art wideband VCOs in
Table I, where the proposed VCO exhibits the largest FTR and
the largest FTR overlap facilitated by MR technique, validating
the robustness of the ultra-wide bandwidth.
In this article, we present a quad-core quad-mode VCO

featuring MR technique and fully symmetrical topology.
By changing the current directions of the tank inductors
via the mode-switching array and incorporating the switched
inductor, four distinct inductance values are realized, enabling
quad-mode operation without electrical coupling. Besides,
with careful consideration of the symmetry in the inductive,
capacitive, and active elements, as well as the routing layout,
mismatches among the VCO cores are signiﬁcantly minimized,
resulting in optimized PN performance. The VCO achieves
an FTR of 113.2% (4.21-to-15.18 GHz), a peak FoMT of
211.6 dBc/Hz and a peak FoMTA of 220.5 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz
offset.

where Cmin and Cmax denote the minimum and maximum values of the tank capacitance, respectively. Thus, MR technique is favored in those multi-core multi-mode VCO designs.

In multi-core multi-mode VCOs, transformer-based resonant tanks are preferred for their design ﬂexibility and area efﬁciency. However, as the number of operation modes increases, transformer design becomes challenging and the coupling network becomes complex, both of which tend to introduce asymmetries across VCO cores. As a result, the asymmetry induced by transformers or even other components inevitably introduces frequency mismatches in multi-core operation, which theoretically degrade the PN performance. Therefore, a fully symmetrical architecture in multi-core multimode VCOs are preferred to eliminate the negative impact on the PN performance.

A substantial number of state-of-the-art triple-mode orquad-mode VCOs have been proposed in recent years. A dualcore triple-mode VCO with a wide FTR of 80.6% and a PN of −137.9 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset from 7.15 GHz is proposed by using Electrical-Magnetic (E-M) mixed coupling in [15]. However, the asymmetrical inductance seen from each core causes inter-core mismatches that degrades the PN. Moreover, the inclusion of additional mode switches and switched capacitor arrays (SCAs) impose extra parasitics, thus reducing the FTR. A quad-core quad-mode VCO in [22] achieves an FTR of 101% and a PN of −133.2 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset from 13.7 GHz by using E-M mixed coupling, whereas the issue of asymmetrical inductance persists, and the parasitics from electric coupling capacitors negatively impact the FTR. Additionally, the non-uniformity of the FTR across each mode is also undesirable. With the same total FTR, a uniform FTR

in each mode yields roughly equal overlaps between adjacent modes, as shown in Fig. 1(a). In contrast, a nonuniform FTR makes the overlaps highly uneven, as shown in Fig. 1(b). This gives rise to two concerns. First, large differences in overlap make the band-decision thresholds difﬁcult to unify and require additional algorithm adaptation, which increases system complexity. Second, under PVT variations, the smaller overlap is more likely to shrink and create a frequency gap between adjacent modes. Other works still suffer from these issues [18], [21]. In summary, although multi-core multimode VCOs have demonstrated superior performance in terms of FTR and PN, issues such as asymmetrical inductance, parasitic-induced FTR reduction, and nonuniform FTR still persist, ultimately degrading the overall performance of the VCOs.

To surmount these issues, this work proposes a quadcore quad-mode VCO that achieves ultra-wide bandwidth and low PN by employing MR technique and fully symmetric architecture, which effectively eliminates the asymmetry and extra parasitics, and ensures a uniform FTR across all modes. This article is organized as follows. Section II presents the structure of the proposed VCO and the operating principles of the four modes. Section III discusses the symmetry of the design and its optimization of performance. Section IV presents the measurement results and Section V draws the conclusion.

In mode-N, as shown in Fig. 4(d), the current in any given core is anti-phase with other three cores, with the switches S1,4, S1,6, S2,3, S2,5, S3,8, S4,7, S5,8, and S6,7 turned on. Based on the current direction in each core, the effective inductance of each core can be derived as L + Mopp for core-1 and -4, L + 2Madj −Mopp for core-2, and L −2Madj −Mopp for core-3. Unlike the other three modes, where the effective inductor for each core is identical, the inductance seen from each core in this mode is varied, leading to signiﬁcant frequency mismatches among four cores. In a multi-core VCO, all cores should be typically designed to be identical to ensure balanced operation. This mismatch in inductance will lead to unequal current distribution among the cores, which in turn causes imbalances in the waveforms among VCO cores. Then the current will ﬂowthrough the lossy switches in order to equalize the energy of the resonators, thereby forcing the VCO to oscillate at the same frequency. This process, however, degrades the tank Q and renders the theoretical 6 dB PN optimization from the quad-core operation unachievable. Therefore, this mode is abandoned. In summary, three distinct equivalent inductance values are realized through a fully symmetrical transformer network composed of four mutually coupled inductors. However, since the difference Lmode,L −Lmode,M exceeds Lmode,M −Lmode,H by 4Mopp, achieving continuous frequency tuning between mode-M and -H may result in a frequency gap between mode-L and -M. Therefore, an additional mode inserted between mode-L and -M is required, which should minimally affect other modes.

VCOs, an embedded switched inductor (Lsw) and a modeswitching (SW) array. The active cores (Core-1, -2, -3, and -4), each composed of cross-coupled transistors, a tail resistor array, a pair of varactors and 6-bit SCA, are identical. The tail resistor array, shown in the bottom-left of Fig. 13(a), consists of a bypass path and a 13-bit programmable resistor bank. It is added to tune the core transconductance Gm versus frequency so that the excess loop gain G X = Gm RT (with RT the tank’s equivalent parallel resistance) remains moderate, which in turn limits ﬂicker noise up-conversion [26]. The 6bit SCA, shown in the top-left of Fig. 13(a), and the MOS varactors provide coarse tuning and continuous ﬁne tuning, respectively. The varactor is implemented using a thick-oxide device, with dimensions of W/L = 32/0.4

m. As the bias increases from 0 to 2.5 V, the varactor capacitance decreases from 35.7 to 15.2 fF (C = 20.5 fF) with Q larger than 29. The SCA exhibits an LSB of 7.7 fF, thereby enabling ﬁne and continuous frequency tuning. With a high Cmax/Cmin ratio preserved and Q kept moderate, the total capacitance ranges from 191.9 to 732.1 fF, and Q remains above 24 at 10 GHz. Each core is connected to its respective inductor ports in a center-symmetric manner, ensuring uniform coupling and balanced performance across all modes.

Furthermore, to maintain uniform capacitive loading at eachport, the SW array is designed with four identical sub-arrays, all positioned at the center of the transformer symmetrically. Each sub-array contains four switches and there are a total of sixteen switches in all. An additional switch is positioned along the routing of the switched inductor to control its on/off state. As discussed above, eight switches need to be turned on and another eight switches need to be turned off in each mode. The switch on-off states in each mode are shown in Fig. 13(b). As observed, these switches are divided into ﬁve groups and are controlled by 5-bit control bits, respectively. In mode-1, Groups-1 and -2 are activated; in mode-2, Groups-1, -2, and -5 are active. Mode-3 enables Group-1 and -3, whereas mode-4 enables Group-3 and -4. Unless otherwise speciﬁed, all other switch groups remain disabled.

Given the careful consideration of the symmetry of theinductive, capacitive, active, and other elements in the quadcore quad-mode VCO, the mismatches among VCO cores are signiﬁcantly minimized, allowing the four single-core VCOs to be well synchronized and achieve optimized PN in all modes.

Given the careful consideration of the symmetry of theinductive, capacitive, active, and other elements in the quadcore quad-mode VCO, the mismatches among VCO cores are signiﬁcantly minimized, allowing the four single-core VCOs to be well synchronized and achieve optimized PN in all modes.
Avoiding Mode Ambiguity

It is known that when the transconductance pairs are sufﬁciently large, the oscillator operates at the frequency where the tank impedance provides sufﬁciently high amplitude with zero phase. When no mode switches are added or the switch size is too small [i.e., large ON-resistance (RON)], multiple frequency points with high impedance amplitude and zero phase may exist. As a result, the operating frequency of the oscillator is not uniquely deﬁned, resulting in mode ambiguity.

Due to the symmetrical property of the proposed transformer, the tank impedance seen from node pairs P1 and P2, P3 and P4, P5 and P6, P7 and P8 is identical. Fig. 14 shows the simulated magnitude and phase responses of the tank impedance seen from the node pair P1 and P2 in the four operation modes, as RON is reduced from 425 to 25 . When RON is 225/425 , as shown by the blue/green dotted curvein Fig. 14, each mode exhibits at least two frequency points where the tank impedance has a sufﬁciently high peak and a zero phase. This implies that the oscillator has the potential to oscillate either at the frequency with the expected maximum Q value or concurrently at multiple resonance frequencies, which are highly undesirable.

To avoid the issues associated with ambiguous modes, it isnecessary to reduce RON by increasing the size of the mode switches. As shown by the solid red curves in Fig. 14, when RON is reduced to 25 , each mode exhibits a uniquely deﬁnedresonant frequency.

Effect of Mismatches Among Cores

While ideal synchronization assumes identical oscillationfrequencies among the cores, practical implementations often suffer from frequency mismatches caused by device variations and layout asymmetries. These mismatches introduce phase errors and amplitude reduction, ultimately degrading the PN performance [21], [27]. Therefore, accurately characterizing and mitigating inter-core mismatches are essential to fully unlock the potential of multi-core VCO designs.

MEASUREMENT RESULTS

The proposed quad-core quad-mode VCO is implementedin 65 nm bulk CMOS with a core chip area of 0.152 mm2, as shown in Fig. 21. Fig. 22 shows the measured PN at 4.28, 8.66, 11.57, and 15.07 GHz, respectively, from four distinct modes. The measured FTR is 113.2% (4.21–15.18 GHz), with the frequency in each mode ranging from 4.21 to 6.24 GHz, 5.62 to 8.66 GHz, 7.52 to 11.6 GHz, and 10.01 to 15.18 GHz, respectively, as shown in Fig. 23. In each mode, the tuning voltage ranges from 0 to 2.5 V. It’s worth noting that the minimum frequency overlap between two adjacent modes is 10.5%, which further validates the robustness of the wide bandwidth. We further report the VCO gain KVCO on this plot at Vtune = 1.2 V . Fig. 24(a) and (b) show the measured PN, FoM and FoMT over the whole FTR, respectively, where the PN is from −108.8 to −120.3 dBc/Hz and −130.7 to −141.4 dBc/Hz at 1 and 10 MHz offsets while the FoM and FoMT vary from 180.0 to 190.5 dBc/Hz and 201.1 to 211.6 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset.

The tank’s effective parallel resistance RT varies by mode, owing to variations in Q across modes. Since mode-1 exhibits the largest Q and thus the largest RT , it requires the smallest gm and hence the lowest current consumption, while the higher frequency and lower Q modes require more. In the proposed design, a programmable tail resistor array is used to adjust the current. In mode-1, a larger tail resistor is used to moderate gm, while smaller resistors are employed in modes-2 and -4 to allow higher gm. The VCO consumes 1.44 to 14.12 mW power under a VDD of 0.4 V, with mode-1: 1.44–3.27 mW; mode-2: 9.51–13.46 mW; mode-3: 11.14–14.10 mW; and mode-4: 12.63–14.12 mW. Although the 0.4 V low supply voltage helps reduce intrinsic power consumption of the VCO, an on-chip regulator is typically required to suppress noise and improve the power supply rejection ratio (PSRR), which results in additional power overhead. Across different modes, the Kpush of the proposed VCO is measured to range from 126 to 297 MHz/V. Since spur level depends on the PSRR, an on-chip regulator with high PSRR is required to keep spurs low. Although magnetic coupling brings Q variations, the tail resistor array ensures the robust start-up and also suppresses ﬂicker noise up-conversion across a wide FTR. This effect is reﬂected in the 1/f3 PN corners in each mode, which span 35–220 kHz (mode-1), 130– 210 kHz (mode-2), 180–600 kHz (mode-3), and 90–750 kHz (mode-4). A lower corner frequency indicates more effective suppression of ﬂicker noise up-conversion. Thanks to the tail resistor, the normalized PN (to 1 GHz) shows good ﬂatness with minimal variations across the whole FTR, as shown in Fig. 24(a). Moreover, Fig. 25 shows that the proposed VCO exhibits the best overall performance in view of FoM and FTR, and the best FoMTA in similar operating frequencies. The results are compared with state-of-the-art wideband VCOs in Table I, where the proposed VCO exhibits the largest FTR and the largest FTR overlap facilitated by MR technique, validating the robustness of the ultra-wide bandwidth.

Since mode-1 exhibits the largest Q and thus the largest RT , it requires the smallest gm and hence the lowest current consumption, while the higher frequency and lower Q modes require more. In the proposed design, a programmable tail resistor array is used to adjust the current. In mode-1, a larger tail resistor is used to moderate gm, while smaller resistors are employed in modes-2 and -4 to allow higher gm. The VCO consumes 1.44 to 14.12 mW power under a VDD of 0.4 V, with mode-1: 1.44–3.27 mW; mode-2: 9.51–13.46 mW; mode-3: 11.14–14.10 mW; and mode-4: 12.63–14.12 mW. Although the 0.4 V low supply voltage helps reduce intrinsic power consumption of the VCO, an on-chip regulator is typically required to suppress noise and improve the power supply rejection ratio (PSRR), which results in additional power overhead. Across different modes, the Kpush of the proposed VCO is measured to range from 126 to 297 MHz/V. Since spur level depends on the PSRR, an on-chip regulator with high PSRR is required to keep spurs low. Although magnetic coupling brings Q variations, the tail resistor array ensures the robust start-up and also suppresses ﬂicker noise up-conversion across a wide FTR. This effect is reﬂected in the 1/f3 PN corners in each mode, which span 35–220 kHz (mode-1), 130– 210 kHz (mode-2), 180–600 kHz (mode-3), and 90–750 kHz (mode-4). A lower corner frequency indicates more effective suppression of ﬂicker noise up-conversion. Thanks to the tail resistor, the normalized PN (to 1 GHz) shows good ﬂatness with minimal variations across the whole FTR, as shown in Fig. 24(a). Moreover, Fig. 25 shows that the proposed VCO exhibits the best overall performance in view of FoM and FTR, and the best FoMTA in similar operating frequencies. The results are compared with state-of-the-art wideband VCOs in Table I, where the proposed VCO exhibits the largest FTR and the largest FTR overlap facilitated by MR technique, validating the robustness of the ultra-wide bandwidth.
CONCLUSION

In this article, we present a quad-core quad-mode VCO featuring MR technique and fully symmetrical topology. By changing the current directions of the tank inductors via the mode-switching array and incorporating the switched inductor, four distinct inductance values are realized, enabling quad-mode operation without electrical coupling. Besides, with careful consideration of the symmetry in the inductive, capacitive, and active elements, as well as the routing layout, mismatches among the VCO cores are signiﬁcantly minimized, resulting in optimized PN performance. The VCO achieves an FTR of 113.2% (4.21-to-15.18 GHz), a peak FoMT of 211.6 dBc/Hz and a peak FoMTA of 220.5 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset.

quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), voltage-controlled oscillators (VCOs) are required to maintain low phase noise (PN). However, achieving wide bandwidth and low PN simultaneously remains a signiﬁcant challenge for VCO designs.

(PN) quad-core quad-mode voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) which features magnetically reconﬁgurable (MR) technique and fully symmetrical architecture. The MR technique, realized through a transformer-based tank integrating an embedded switched inductor, leverages varying core excitation currents to achieve four distinct equivalent inductances, thereby enabling quad-mode operation. This approach avoids the frequency tuning range (FTR) compromise encountered when using capacitive tuning elements in multi-mode tanks. Furthermore, the fully symmetrical characteristics of the inductive, capacitive, and active elements, along with the routing layout, minimize mismatches among the VCO cores, ensuring effective synchronization of the four single-core VCOs and optimizing the PN in quad-core operation. The proposed quad-core quad-mode VCO achieves an FTR of 113.2% (4.21 to 15.18 GHz), a PN of −141.4 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset from 4.28 GHz, a peak ﬁgure-of-merit (FoM) of 190.5 dBc/Hz, a peak FoMT of 211.6 dBc/Hz and a peak FoMTA of 220.5 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset.

Compared to the scheme that uses multiple individual VCOs for multi-band operation, mode-switching technique summarized in [1] provides a more efﬁcient solution, enabling multi-band coverage with reduced area and lower power consumption. The switched-inductors or switched-transformers techniques are favorable to achieve wide bandwidth by utilizing multiple effective inductance values [2], [3], [4]. Although these techniques can broaden the bandwidth effectively in a simple manner, the ON-resistance of the switches degrades the Q factor of the tank, thus signiﬁcantly deteriorating the PN.
Recently, coupling multiple VCO cores operating at different modes via mode switches has been demonstrated to be a promising method to simultaneously achieve low PN and wide FTR.
